title: Sorting the Problem
focus: Sort first and half the problem disappears. Then the week's hardest idea: patience sorting.

cards.title: Interval Merging
cards.trigger: A list of [start, end] pairs and a question about overlap, coverage or conflict.
cards.recall: Write the merge from memory. Then answer: you sorted by start, so what is the single comparison that decides merge versus append, and why is `>=` versus `>` a question you must ask the interviewer?
useWhen: Merge overlapping intervals
Insert an interval into a sorted non-overlapping list
Count how many intervals a point is covered by
Remove the fewest intervals to remove all overlap, sort by END for that one
Meeting room conflicts and calendar booking
template: if out and start <= out[-1][1]:        # overlap or touch
out[-1][1] = max(out[-1][1], end)  # max, not end
# Non-overlapping: keep the most intervals -> greedy by EARLIEST END
keyInsights: `max(out[-1][1], end)` matters because a fully contained interval must not shrink the merged one
Sort by start to merge. Sort by end to schedule the most. Two different problems, two different keys
Whether [1,2] and [2,3] overlap is a real ambiguity. Ask, do not assume
cards.trap: 'Intervals arrive one at a time and you must answer after each.' Sorting is gone. You need an ordered structure keyed by start, and that is the real question.

cards.title: Heap Scheduling
patterns: Rooms as a heap of end times
cards.trigger: Assign a stream of jobs to slots or resources, always taking the currently most urgent.
cards.recall: Write the meeting rooms solution with a min-heap of end times from memory. Then answer: why does the heap size at any moment equal the number of concurrent meetings?
useWhen: Minimum meeting rooms, maximum concurrency
Task scheduler with a cooldown between identical tasks
CPU or worker assignment by shortest job or highest priority
Reorganise a string so no two identical characters are adjacent
Merge k streams by next-available timestamp
template: # Minimum rooms: heap holds END times of live meetings
heapq.heappop(live)        # a room freed up before this start
# Task scheduler, closed form: the most frequent task sets the skeleton
ties = sum(1 for v in freq.values() if v == top)
keyInsights: The heap holds end times, so its size is exactly the number of overlapping meetings. The answer is the maximum size
Popping at most one per iteration is enough, because you only need one room for the one meeting starting now
The chalkboard alternative is a sweep line over sorted start and end events. Know both and say which is cleaner here
cards.trap: 'Which rooms specifically?' The count version throws away identity. You need to store (end, room_id) and recycle ids, and that is a real design change.

cards.title: Balance and Height
cards.trigger: A question about tree shape rather than tree contents.
cards.recall: Write the balanced check that runs in O(n) from memory. Then answer: the naive version calls height inside isBalanced and is O(n^2), so what does the sentinel return buy you?
useWhen: Is this tree height balanced
Build a balanced BST from a sorted array
Minimum depth, careful, a one-child node is not a leaf
Check completeness or perfectness for a heap-backed tree
Any question about the O(h) guarantee holding
template: # O(n): return -1 as 'already unbalanced below me'
# Sorted array -> balanced BST: the middle is always the root
keyInsights: The sentinel fuses 'compute height' and 'check balance' into one pass, turning O(n^2) into O(n)
Minimum depth is the classic off-by-one: a node with one child is not a leaf, so you cannot just take min of both
Every self-balancing tree, AVL and red-black, exists to keep this height invariant so O(h) stays O(log n)
cards.trap: 'What does a real AVL do on insert?' Rotations. You do not need to code them, but you must be able to say single versus double and which case triggers which.

cards.title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
cards.trigger: Longest chain under an ordering constraint, where the elements need not be adjacent.
cards.recall: Write the O(n log n) version from memory. Then answer the thing nearly everyone gets wrong: is the `tails` array itself a valid LIS, and if not, why is its length still correct?
useWhen: Longest increasing or decreasing subsequence
Russian doll envelopes, after sorting one dimension
Maximum chain of pairs
Minimum deletions to make an array sorted, n minus LIS
Box stacking and any 2D dominance chain
template: # O(n^2): dp[i] = LIS length ending exactly at i
# O(n log n): tails[k] = smallest possible tail of an increasing run of length k+1
i = bisect.bisect_left(tails, x)   # bisect_right for non-decreasing
# Envelopes: sort by width asc, height DESC on ties, then LIS on heights
keyInsights: `tails` is not an actual subsequence. Only its length is meaningful. Claiming otherwise is a common and visible error
`bisect_left` gives strictly increasing, `bisect_right` gives non-decreasing. That one word in the prompt picks the function
The height-descending tie-break on envelopes is what stops equal widths from chaining. Without it the answer is too large
cards.trap: 'Reconstruct the subsequence.' You must record a predecessor index per element alongside the tails array. The length-only version cannot be retrofitted.

cards.title: All-Pairs Shortest Path
cards.trigger: You need distances between every pair, and the vertex count is small, roughly under 400.
cards.recall: Write the triple loop from memory. Then answer the one thing that matters: why must `k` be the outermost loop, and what does the algorithm compute if you put it innermost?
useWhen: All-pairs shortest path on a dense small graph
Find the city with the fewest reachable neighbours within a threshold
Transitive closure, who can reach whom, with booleans
Detect a negative cycle, any dist[i][i] below zero
Precompute a distance matrix once and answer many queries
template: # dist is V x V, dist[i][i] = 0, dist[u][v] = w, everything else INF
for k in range(V):                 # k MUST be outermost
# Negative cycle: any i with dist[i][i] < 0
# Transitive closure: replace + with and, min with or

problem.name: Find the City With the Smallest Number of Neighbors

keyInsights: After iteration k, dist holds shortest paths using only vertices 0..k as intermediates. k outermost is what makes that induction hold
It handles negative edges. It does not handle negative cycles, it only detects them
V^3 at V = 400 is 64 million, which is the practical ceiling. Above that, run Dijkstra from every source
cards.trap: 'The graph has 10,000 nodes.' V^3 is a trillion. Say the number out loud and switch to V rounds of Dijkstra.
